analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts through nonpartisan agencies instead of politicians.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Constitution subcommittee from March 2014 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state, after the 2020 census, to hand the drawing of congressional district maps to a nonpartisan staff agency in the state legislature, working with a small advisory commission. That agency would be barred from considering where incumbents live, how districts have voted in the past, or the party affiliation of residents. The state legislature could only approve or reject the resulting map — not rewrite it — and if two proposed maps were rejected, the state's highest court would draw the lines.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where district lines have been drawn to protect one party or to shield incumbents. Districts would be compact, keep communities together where practicable, and could no longer be shaped around politicians' home addresses or voters' party histories. Voters would also get public hearings on any proposed map.

how_it_helps.text: The agency drawing the maps is legally barred from considering the residence of House incumbents, the voting history of a district, or the party affiliation of its residents, except as needed to comply with the Voting Rights Act [S3].
Maps must follow objective criteria: equal population within one percent, contiguity, compactness, and keeping political subdivisions together where practicable [S3].

The state legislature could only approve or reject the agency's map — the first two plans could not be amended — and had to act within days, with public hearings and written explanations required for any rejection [S2] [S3].
If the legislature rejected two proposed maps, the state's highest court would take over and draw the map using the same neutral criteria [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the politicians who currently control map-drawing. Their districts could no longer be tailored around them, and partisan majorities in state legislatures would lose the power to draw congressional lines to their own advantage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent House members and legislative map-drawers

drawbacks.text: The commission's five members are all appointed by legislative majority and minority leaders, so politicians would still pick the reviewers even though the map-drawers themselves are nonpartisan [S3].

Requiring districts to vary by no more than one percent in population is stricter than existing law and could force splits of towns and counties that the contiguity and community-keeping rules try to avoid [S3].

It is a federal mandate on state governments, an approach critics commonly challenge as intruding on state control of elections, and it leaves state and local district maps entirely under the old system [S3].
It would not take effect until redistricting after the 2020 census, so it offered no help for the lines drawn that decade [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: voters get maps drawn by neutral staff under written criteria, while sitting politicians lose a tool they have used to protect their own seats. The main weaknesses are that the review commission is still chosen by legislative leaders and that the federal one-percent population rule could create awkward district shapes. On balance the bill targeted a real, self-serving practice — legislators drawing their own congressional districts — with a workable, if imperfect, alternative.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Constitution and Civil Justice subcommittee, and no hearing or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Braley of Iowa introduced the bill on January 16, 2014, joined by one cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On March 20, 2014, it was referred to the subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, the last action of any kind [S5].
The bill received no committee vote, no floor action, and no vote in the Senate before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the state legislators who control redistricting keep the power to draw congressional maps to their own advantage, because the reform never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Braley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require nonpartisan state agencies to draw congressional district maps.

for.name: Rep. David Loebsack
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 20, 2014 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the cosponsor were Iowa Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so the broader partisan divide over redistricting reform never showed up in the record.

industries.note: Map-drawers could no longer consider where incumbents live, so districts could not be quietly tailored to protect them. Their interest in keeping that protection runs against voters' interest in competitive, compact districts.

industries.industry: State legislative majorities and party organizations
industries.note: Control over drawing congressional maps would shift from partisan legislators to a nonpartisan agency, and the legislature could only accept or reject the result. Parties lose their ability to engineer district lines for seats.
